questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman presented with a productive cough as well as a painful swollen nose with copious discharge. She reported a biphasic illness, as the current symptoms had been preceded by recovery from a 1-week history of malaise, fever, headache, and myalgia. She had a history of osteoarthritis but did not take any regular medications. She worked as an equine vet. On examination her temperature was 37.5°C, her respiratory rate was 18 breaths/minute, and her oxygen saturations were 97% on room air. Her nose and surrounding facial skin were moderately swollen, and she had palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. Flexible nasal endoscopy was performed, followed by bronchoscopy, which revealed multiple necrotic ulcers in the mucosal lining of the tracheobronchial tree. Investigations: Biopsies were taken and sent for microscopy and culture Results: gram-negative bacilli with rounded ends seen on direct microscopy Chest X-ray was unremarkable
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Burkholderia mallei Clinically, this patient has glanders. She has the potential for occupational exposure, and the nasal involvement and tracheobronchial ulceration reflect likely inhalational transmission of Burkholderia mallei from one of her equine patients. The biphasic illness may also be characteristic. Treatment options are limited by the facultative intracellular nature of B. mallei, as well as multiple antimicrobial resistance mechanisms. First-line options are ceftazidime, imipenem, or meropenem, with or without trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q44

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man was admitted with new-onset urinary retention following 72 hours of dysuria and 1 week of malaise. He had osteoarthritis of the right knee. He was not on any regular medication. He had returned from a 4-week holiday to northern Australia 2 weeks before he developed symptoms. His temperature was 38.3°C, heart rate 110 beats per minute. Blood cultures were taken. Digital rectal examination revealed a tender boggy prostate. He was given a single dose of gentamicin 5 mg/kg and started on regular co-amoxiclav, 1.2 g TDS IV . Investigations: Transrectal ultrasound of prostate: large prostatic abscess, maximum diameter 4.5 cm CT scan of abdomen and pelvis: small abscess in upper pole of left kidney, maximum diameter 2.4 cm Random glucose 17.3 mmol/L Glycosylated hemoglobin 12.8% Blood cultures: gram-negative rods at 14 hours Colonies on Ashdown agar: oxidase positive; bipolar staining on Gram stain (see images) A B C He was switched to meropenem. After 7 days he was still regularly having temperatures >38°C but was cardiovascularly stable.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Continue current treatment Melioidosis is characterized by difficulty in eradicating the causative organisms. Fever clearance is often slow (median fever clearance time of 9 days) and without evidence of clinical deterioration is not normally sufficient to indicate the need for a change in therapy. A patient who has clinical deterioration or persistently positive blood cultures should be viewed as failing treatment, at which stage the need for imaging, drainage of collections, and change in antimicrobial therapy should be considered. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q41

questions.question: A patient returned 3 days ago from an adventure trip to northern Australia. He has severe, rapidly progressive right upper lobe pneumonia and falls into septic shock. He is not responding to ceftriaxone and vancomycin, and sputum shows gram-negative bacilli.
questions.question_raw: You see a patient who returned 3 days ago from an adventure trip to northern Australia. He has severe pneumonia of the right upper lobe, rapidly progressive, and falls into septic shock. Not responding to CTX and vanco, sputum shows GNB.

parts.text: Name the most likely etiologic agent.
Name the recommended induction (initial intensive) therapy and duration.
Name the recommended eradication treatment and duration.

parts_raw.text: Name the most likely etiologic agent
Name the recommended induction therapy and duration
Name the recommended eradication treatment and duration

questions.model_answer:
a) Burkholderia pseudomallei (melioidosis) — acute septicemic pneumonia in a returned traveller from the Top End of northern Australia, an endemic focus.
b) Initial intensive IV therapy: meropenem (up to 1 g q8h) — drug of choice for melioidosis septic shock — or ceftazidime (up to 2 g q6h); minimum 10–14 days, and because this is ICU pneumonia with septic shock the intensive phase should run at least 4 weeks (longer if slow response or positive cultures at day 7). TMP-SMX may be added.
c) Eradication: oral TMP-SMX (up to 320/1600 mg q12h) for a minimum of 3 months.

cohort_answer.text:
Most likely etiologic agent: Burkholderia pseudomallei
Induction therapy: Ceftazidime or Meropenem x at least 14 days
Eradication treatment: TMP-SMX x 3–6 mos (Redbook/CDC). Amoxicillin clavulanate and doxycycline are second-line and may be associated with a higher rate of relapse.

questions.model_answer:
a) Burkholderia pseudomallei.
b) (1) Northeast Thailand and (2) the Top End of the Northern Territory of Australia (the two most important endemic foci; Southeast Asia broadly and northern Australia).
c) B. pseudomallei is readily misidentified by commercial systems as a Pseudomonas or other Burkholderia species, so alerting the lab ensures correct identification (e.g. selective Ashdown medium) and appropriate biosafety handling given the risk of laboratory-acquired infection.
d) (1) Ceftazidime (up to 2 g q6h) (2) Meropenem (up to 1 g q8h) (3) Imipenem (up to 1 g q6h) — any one may be combined with TMP-SMX.

questions.question_raw: PM Q6. Middle aged man back from 'adventure travel' in north Australia, now in ICU with fever, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and shock. Blood culture shows Gram-negative bacillus.

parts_raw.text: a) What is the pathogen?
b) What would be your empiric therapy?

questions.model_answer:
a) Burkholderia pseudomallei (melioidosis).
b) Meropenem (up to 1 g q8h) — drug of choice in septic shock — or ceftazidime (up to 2 g q6h) IV.
c) Two-phase therapy: (1) Initial intensive IV meropenem or ceftazidime for a minimum of 10–14 days, extended to at least 4 weeks for ICU/severe pneumonia (longer for deep-seated collections, osteomyelitis 6 weeks, CNS 8 weeks), optionally with TMP-SMX; then (2) oral eradication with TMP-SMX for a minimum of 3 months (6 months for osteomyelitis or CNS disease).

cohort_answer.text:
Burkholderia pseudomallei
Carbapenem (imipenem/cilastatin or Meropenem) or Ceftazidime 2g IV q6h
Induction: Carbapenem + TMP/SMX (recommended for neurologic, cutaneous, bone, joint, prostatic melioidosis) x2-8 weeks. Consolidation: TMP/SMX x3-6 months (6 months for CNS/bone, 3 months other)

questions.question: For each of the following marine-associated pathogens - Aeromonas, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Vibrio vulnificus, Streptococcus iniae, Mycobacterium marinum, and Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - describe the water exposure, clinical syndrome, and treatment.
questions.question_raw: Bonus: Describe type of water exposure, clinical syndrome, and treatment for: Aeromonas, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Vibrio vulnificus, Streptococcus iniae, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae

parts.text: Describe the type of water exposure for each.
Describe their clinical syndrome.
Treatment for each.
Prophylactic therapy (assuming wound exposure).

parts_raw.text: Describe type of water exposure for each
Describe their clinical syndrome
Treatment for each
Prophylactic therapy (assuming wound exposure)

questions.model_answer:
a) Water exposure: Aeromonas - fresh/brackish water; Burkholderia pseudomallei - fresh water/wet soil; Vibrio vulnificus - warm salt/brackish seawater (or raw oysters); Streptococcus iniae - fresh water (tilapia/fish handling); Mycobacterium marinum - fresh or salt water (aquariums, fish); Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - salt water (fish/shellfish handling).
b) Clinical syndrome: Aeromonas - cellulitis, myonecrosis, ecthyma gangrenosum; B. pseudomallei - melioidosis (skin abscesses/ulcers, pneumonia, sepsis, worse in cirrhotics/diabetics); V. vulnificus - rapidly progressive necrotizing cellulitis with hemorrhagic bullae, primary septicemia; S. iniae - cellulitis/bacteremia; M. marinum - indolent papules/nodules with sporotrichoid spread ('fish-tank granuloma'); E. rhusiopathiae - erysipeloid of Rosenbach (subacute cellulitis of the fingers/hand).
c) Treatment: Aeromonas - fluoroquinolone or third-gen cephalosporin +/- doxycycline; B. pseudomallei - ceftazidime or a carbapenem (meropenem) then eradication with TMP-SMX; V. vulnificus - third-gen cephalosporin + doxycycline (or fluoroquinolone) plus surgical debridement; S. iniae - penicillin/beta-lactam; M. marinum - clarithromycin plus ethambutol +/- rifampin; E. rhusiopathiae - penicillin or ampicillin.
d) Prophylaxis (wound exposure): no firm guideline; irrigate/debride, ensure tetanus prophylaxis, and consider empiric coverage for high-risk wounds (deep punctures, immunocompromised/liver disease) - e.g. a fluoroquinolone or first-gen cephalosporin, adding doxycycline for salt-water exposure to cover Vibrio and metronidazole for soil/sewage contamination.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only V. vulnificus is covered in this chapter; the other five pathogens' water exposure, syndromes, treatment and wound prophylaxis are from established knowledge/IDSA SSTI and species-specific chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Water type: Aeromonas - fresh water; Burkholderia pseudomallei - fresh water; Vibrio vulnificus - salt water; Streptococcus iniae - fresh water; Mycobacterium marinum - salt or fresh water; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - salt water. Clinical: Aeromonas - cellulitis/myonecrosis/rhabdo/ecthyma gangrenosum, men:women 3:1, also leech-associated; Burkholderia pseudomallei - melioidosis, intracellular GNB, skin ulcers/abscesses failing PO abx, worse in cirrhotics; Vibrio vulnificus - rapidly progressive infection, necrotizing infections, hemorrhagic bullae, linked to raw oysters/puncture wounds; Streptococcus iniae - assoc with tilapia fish farming, impetigo/cellulitis; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - erysipeloid of Rosenbach, subacute cellulitis of fingers/hands; Mycobacterium marinum - indolent (mean incubation 21d), papules/nodules progressing to ulceration/scar, sporotrichoid spread. Treatment: Aeromonas – Doxycycline + FQ/3rd gen Ceph; Burkholderia pseudomallei – Ceftazidime or carbapenem; Vibrio vulnificus – Doxycycline + 3rd gen ceph; Streptococcus iniae – beta-lactam; Mycobacterium marinum – Clarithromycin + Ethambutol/Rifampin; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae – penicillin/ampicillin/cephalexin. Prophylaxis: no clear guideline; reasonable for deep puncture/laceration, wounds needing surgical repair, wounds with water exposure outside treated pools, crush injury, vascular/lymphatic compromise, hands/feet/face/genital area, near bone/joint, immunocompromised/diabetic/liver disease. Empiric: 1st gen cephalosporin OR clindamycin + fluoroquinolone; salt water add doxycycline; soil/sewage add metronidazole; wash wound, debride, tetanus prophylaxis
